title: 14. Areas of Triangles and Quadrilaterals (Heron’s Formula)

q.t: For a triangle with sides a, b, c, the semi-perimeter s is:
q.e: ‘Semi’ means half: half of the perimeter.

q.t: Find the semi-perimeter of a triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm (in cm).
Heron’s formula for the area of a triangle is:
q.e: It gives the area from the three sides alone — no height needed.

Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 4 cm (in cm²).

q.e: The legs are base and height.

q.t: Find the semi-perimeter of a triangle with sides 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm (in cm).
The area of an equilateral triangle of side a is:
q.e: Its height is (√3/2)a, so the area is ½ × a × (√3/2)a.

q.t: A triangle has sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm. Find its longest altitude (in cm).
q.e: Area = 36. The longest altitude falls on the shortest side: 2 × 36 ÷ 9.

q.e: These are double 13, 14, 15, so the area is 4 × 84.

q.t: A trapezium has parallel sides 25 cm and 10 cm and non-parallel sides 14 cm and 13 cm. Find its area (in cm²).
q.e: Cut off a parallelogram to leave a triangle with sides 15, 14, 13 (area 84). Its height on 15 is 11.2 cm. Area = ½ × 35 × 11.2.

q.t: A rhombus has perimeter 80 cm and one diagonal 24 cm. Find its area (in cm²).
q.e: Side 20, half-diagonal 12, so the other half is 16 and that diagonal 32. ½ × 24 × 32.

q.t: Each side of a triangle is doubled. By what percent does its area increase?
q.e: s and each of (s − a), (s − b), (s − c) double, so the product under the root is × 16 and the area × 4 — an increase of 300%.

A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. Find the radius of the circle inscribed in it (in cm).
q.e: Area = r × s (the three small triangles with height r). 84 = r × 21.
